D9 · DSP L08: The Unilateral z-Transform, plus Mixed z-Domain Practice

Why this matters in the exam: L08 lists “Apply unilateral z-transform method to find system responses” as one of its four learning outcomes, and slides 13–14 teach it with one worked example. L05–L10 have never been tested, so you have no past-paper evidence for its marks. The closest evidence is Sample Test 1 Q4: 7 of its 20 marks went to solving an LCCDE. The unilateral transform is the z-domain way to solve that same kind of question when the system is not initially at rest. In the course files, only T3 Q4 has non-zero initial conditions, and it was solved in the time domain. Expect a short multi-part question (roughly 4–8 marks) that gives you an LCCDE, , and an input, and asks for . It may also ask you to split the answer into its zero-input and zero-state parts.

1. The core ideas

1.1 Definition (L08 slide 13)

Point What it means for you
Only samples are summed. If for , then , the ordinary (bilateral) transform from L07. All your L07 pairs still work for causal signals.
The inverse is always causal. Every partial fraction inverts with . There is no ROC choice to make.
A two-sided signal loses its part. For example, only.
What it is for The shift property carries the initial conditions into the algebra. In the lecturer’s words, there is “simply no way to do so for the 2-sided transform”.

1.4 Pairs and checks you will use

Pair or check Use Trap
every simple pole none: it is always the causal form here
a repeated pole (input pole = system pole, or a double root of ) Do not confuse it with . Both follow from the L07 differentiation property.
Residue: partial-fraction coefficients (L08 slide 4) Substitute , not .
Initial value: (L07 slide 14) Set in . Free 1-mark check. It must equal from the recursion.
Step steady state: coefficient of Use it when all poles are inside the unit circle. It is meaningless for unstable systems.

2. The method

Recognise the question type. Look for these cues:

  • “initial conditions , ”
  • “the system is not initially at rest”
  • “use the one-sided (unilateral) z-transform”
  • “find the zero-input / zero-state / total response”

If the system is “initially at rest”, all ICs are zero. The question is then just from L08 (Playbook A still works; skip step 3).

Playbook A: total response by the unilateral z-transform

  1. Standard form. Put on the left with coefficient 1, all terms on the left and all terms on the right. Read off and . Note which are zero.
  2. Transform term by term. Use the shift rules for the terms. For a causal input, . Write from L07, e.g. .
  3. Substitute the ICs and simplify the IC polynomial . Keep the signs.
  4. Isolate: . Factor into . Its roots are the L04 characteristic roots.
  5. Tidy. Combine over one denominator if you want the total in one step. Look for a factor that cancels, because ICs often cancel a pole. Make sure the fraction is proper in . If it is not, long-divide first; the quotient gives terms.
  6. Partial fractions. Use the residue formula for simple poles. For a double pole , use . Get from the residue of the squared factor. Get by setting , which gives the constant-term equation.
  7. Invert with causal pairs only. Write the answer for (or multiply by ).
  8. Check. Compute (and ) by recursion from the LCCDE. Compare with your closed form and with .

Playbook B: zero-input and zero-state split

  1. . Invert it. Its terms use only the system poles.
  2. . Invert it.
  3. Check that equals your total, coefficient by coefficient.
  4. Optional time-domain check of the zero-input part: must reproduce and directly. The homogeneous equation holds for every , so you may fit at .

Playbook C: cross-check with the L04 time-domain method

  1. Find the modes from the roots of . These are the same as the poles of .
  2. Guess with the same form as the input, then solve for its constant.
  3. Find and by recursion using the ICs.
  4. Fit at . The result must equal the z-domain total.

Use the time-domain constants only for the total. They are not the zero-input coefficients, because they also contain the natural-mode part of the zero-state response.

Playbook D: “choose the IC so that a mode disappears”

  1. Leave the unknown IC as a symbol, say , and get over one denominator.
  2. The mode disappears when the numerator vanishes at . Solve that for .
  3. Cancel the factor and invert what is left.

Playbook E: mixed z-domain questions (L07–L08 together)

  1. Poles and zeros: write in powers of and include and (L07 slides 16–17).
  2. Possible ROCs are rings bounded by pole radii. Each pole is causal if the ROC lies outside it and anti-causal if the ROC lies inside it (L08 slide 4).
  3. Stability means the ROC contains . A system is both causal and stable if and only if all its poles are inside the unit circle (L08 slide 8).
  4. If the question then adds ICs or “starting at ”, switch to the unilateral transform. That forces the causal ROC.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Dropping the term in . It is , three terms.
  • Sign slips moving IC terms across. Write first, then move . In Example 1, , so it enters with a minus sign.
  • Adding IC terms for the input. A causal input that “starts at ” has . Only terms get initial conditions. MX3(d) below shows why this matters.
  • Skipping a zero coefficient correctly. If (for example ), there is no term from . But still appears through .
  • Fitting the total time-domain solution at . The forced solution is only valid for . Fit totals at obtained by recursion. Only the zero-input part can be fitted at .
  • Calling the L04 constants “the zero-input response”. They are not. See Example 1: , while the zero-input coefficient is .
  • Using the wrong pair for a double pole. , not . A double pole appears whenever the input has the same pole as the system (Q6, Example 3).
  • Choosing a non-causal ROC. The unilateral output is causal by construction, so every term inverts to . The ROC choices from L08 slide 4 apply only to the bilateral transform.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

UNILATERAL z-TRANSFORM (L08 s13-14)
X+(z) = sum_{n>=0} x(n) z^-n     (= X(z) if x causal; inverse ALWAYS causal, no ROC choice)
y(n-1) -> z^-1 Y + y(-1)
y(n-2) -> z^-2 Y + z^-1 y(-1) + y(-2)        <- don't drop the z^-1 y(-1) term
x(n-k) -> z^-k X   for input starting at n=0  (x(-1)=x(-2)=0)
x(n+1) -> zX - z x(0)

2nd order: A(z)Y + I(z) = B(z)X,  I(z) = a1 y(-1) + a2 y(-2) + a2 y(-1) z^-1
  Y_zs = B X / A = H X   (input+system poles)     Y_zi = -I / A  (system poles only)
  y = y_zi + y_zs

PAIRS  p^n u(n) <-> 1/(1-p z^-1)      (n+1)p^n u(n) <-> 1/(1-p z^-1)^2
       n p^n u(n) <-> p z^-1/(1-p z^-1)^2
RESIDUE A_i = (1-p_i z^-1)Y |_{z^-1 = 1/p_i}; double pole: C from squared factor,
        B from z^-1 = 0 (constant terms)
CHECKS  y(0) = Y(z^-1 = 0) = recursion value;  y(1) by recursion
        step steady state = H(1) (stable only)
L04 CHECK  modes + y_p, fit at y(0),y(1) from recursion (NOT at y(-1),y(-2))
           only y_zi may be fitted at n=-1,-2.  L04 constants != y_zi coefficients
KILL A MODE p: numerator of Y = 0 at z^-1 = 1/p  -> solve for unknown IC
ROC (bilateral): causal |z|>max pole; stable <=> ROC contains |z|=1;
                 causal & stable <=> all poles inside unit circle
